triage.name: Contrast-induced nephropathy
triage.reason: Iatrogenic cause of acute kidney injury with a recognizable timeline after contrast exposure; students can work through risk factors, urinalysis and creatinine trend.

demographics: Occurs in patients undergoing procedures that use iodinated contrast, so the age distribution follows that of cardiac catheterization, CT angiography and contrast-enhanced CT
More common in hospitalized and critically ill patients than in outpatients

risk_factors.text: Heart failure or low ejection fraction
High volume or high osmolality of iodinated contrast used
Intra-arterial contrast administration, especially first-pass renal exposure

exposures: Iodinated contrast media given for CT, angiography, cardiac catheterization or another contrast-enhanced study
Recent exposure usually within 24–72 hours before presentation

chief_complaints.text: I haven't been making much urine since my scan
I just feel wiped out and puffy
I'm short of breath and my legs are swollen

hpi.onset: Gradual, beginning 24–72 hours after receiving iodinated contrast; often noticed first by nursing staff as falling urine output
hpi.duration: Typically 3–10 days, with creatinine peaking around 3–5 days and returning toward baseline within 1–3 weeks
hpi.progression: Urine output drops over 1–2 days, creatinine rises, and the patient may develop edema, weight gain and breathlessness; most recover, but some need dialysis
hpi.location: Not focal; generalized fluid retention and malaise
hpi.quality: Insidious and nonspecific; many patients feel only mildly unwell while their labs worsen
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate in most cases; severe when oliguria, volume overload or uremia develop
hpi.timing: Continuous after contrast exposure; oliguria may be transient
aggravating: Poor oral intake or ongoing fluid losses
relieving: Supportive care with careful fluid balance

associated_symptoms.text: Swelling of the legs and ankles
Shortness of breath, especially lying flat

pertinent_negatives: Recent sore throat or skin infection
Exposure to a known nephrotoxin other than contrast
Symptoms of prostatic obstruction such as hesitancy or dribbling

argues_against: Fever with chills suggesting infection or sepsis

positives.text: Swelling of the legs and ankles
Shortness of breath when lying flat

argues_against: Chest pain suggesting acute coronary syndrome rather than contrast nephropathy
Gastrointestinal bleeding as a cause of volume depletion and rising creatinine
Flank pain or hematuria suggesting urinary obstruction or glomerulonephritis
Focal neurologic deficits suggesting a primary neurologic cause
Rash or purpura suggesting vasculitis or thrombotic microangiopathy

atypical.how_it_differs: May present only with confusion, falls or poor appetite; oliguria is easily missed because urine output is not measured at home.
Patients with pre-existing chronic kidney disease have less reserve, so a smaller contrast load causes a larger creatinine rise and they are more likely to need dialysis.
Diabetic patients often have baseline kidney disease and may have blunted symptoms; the creatinine rise can be mistaken for diabetic nephropathy progression.

Contrast-induced nephropathy is uncommon in children with normal kidneys; when it occurs it follows high-dose contrast for cardiac catheterization or malignancy imaging and presents with reduced urine output.

general.mild: Comfortable or mildly fatigued; no distress at rest
general.moderate: Fatigued, mildly ill-appearing; may have dependent edema
general.severe: Ill-appearing, dyspneic when lying flat, visibly volume-overloaded
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic or confused, in respiratory distress from pulmonary edema

findings.maneuver: Press firmly over the dorsum of the foot and the medial malleolus for several seconds
findings.finding: Pitting edema of the lower extremities

findings.maneuver: Inspect the internal jugular vein with the patient at 30–45 degrees
Auscultate the apex with the bell
Compare current weight with the pre-procedure weight
Ask the patient to hold both arms outstretched with wrists extended
Measure temperature and inspect for systemic signs
Inspect the skin over the trunk and extremities

findings.finding: No abdominal tenderness or palpable bladder

labs.caveat: The diagnosis rests on a rise in creatinine of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours of contrast, or a 1.5-fold rise from baseline within 7 days; a single value means little without the pre-contrast baseline.
Rises with the creatinine; a BUN/creatinine ratio above 20 favors a prerenal component from volume depletion.
Hyperkalemia is the main immediate danger; watch for peaked T waves on ECG.
Metabolic acidosis from reduced renal acid excretion.
Dilutional hyponatremia from impaired free-water excretion.
Isosthenuria (fixed specific gravity near 1.010) reflects loss of concentrating ability; a high specific gravity with a high BUN/creatinine ratio instead points to prerenal azotemia.
Mild proteinuria is common; heavy proteinuria or an active sediment suggests glomerulonephritis instead.
Muddy brown granular casts support acute tubular injury but are not specific to contrast; their absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
A few red cells can follow catheterization; numerous dysmorphic red cells or red cell casts point to glomerulonephritis.
Anemia of chronic kidney disease or dilution from fluid retention; a falling hemoglobin with schistocytes suggests hemolysis or thrombotic microangiopathy.
Thrombocytopenia with anemia and rising creatinine should raise concern for thrombotic microangiopathy rather than contrast nephropathy.
Helps separate volume overload from contrast nephropathy versus cardiogenic pulmonary edema when the patient is dyspneic.

findings.finding: Sinus bradycardia or junctional rhythm from hyperkalemia
Sinus tachycardia from volume depletion, pain or underlying illness

imaging.preferred_when: When obstruction or chronic kidney disease is suspected, or when the cause of the acute kidney injury is unclear

findings.text: Increased echogenicity of the renal cortex
Small, shrunken kidneys suggesting pre-existing chronic kidney disease
Hydronephrosis indicating obstruction rather than contrast nephropathy

imaging.study: Duplex ultrasound of the renal arteries
imaging.preferred_when: When renal artery stenosis is suspected as an alternative cause of worsening kidney function

findings.text: Tardus-parvus waveform or elevated peak systolic velocity suggesting renal artery stenosis

imaging.study: Non-contrast CT of the abdomen and pelvis
imaging.preferred_when: When a stone or other structural cause of obstruction is suspected and ultrasound is nondiagnostic

imaging.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

findings.text: Avoid in the acute phase; additional iodinated contrast can worsen kidney injury and rarely changes management

imaging.study: Magnetic resonance angiography of the renal arteries
imaging.preferred_when: When vascular anatomy is needed and iodinated contrast must be avoided

initial.why: Establishes the creatinine rise, potassium, bicarbonate and BUN; the core of diagnosis and monitoring
Looks for anemia, thrombocytopenia or leukocytosis suggesting an alternative cause
Sediment and specific gravity help separate acute tubular injury from prerenal, glomerular or interstitial disease
Excludes obstruction and assesses kidney size and chronicity
initial.only_if: obstruction, chronic kidney disease or an unclear cause of acute kidney injury is suspected

confirmatory.why: A rise of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours of contrast, or a 1.5-fold rise from baseline within 7 days, with no other cause, confirms the diagnosis

supporting.why: Helps distinguish volume overload from heart failure when the patient is dyspneic
Falling hemoglobin with schistocytes suggests hemolysis or thrombotic microangiopathy
Thrombocytopenia raises concern for thrombotic microangiopathy

supporting.test: Duplex ultrasound of the renal arteries
supporting.why: Evaluates for renal artery stenosis when vascular disease is suspected

not_indicated.test: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast
not_indicated.why: Additional iodinated contrast can worsen kidney injury and is rarely needed
No role in acute kidney injury
Not needed unless abdominal pain suggests pancreatitis
Only relevant if pregnancy would change management or imaging decisions

decision_points: Compare the current creatinine with the pre-contrast baseline; the diagnosis depends on the change, not a single value
Review all nephrotoxic medications and stop them when possible
Assess volume status before giving fluids; hypovolemia worsens injury but overload can cause pulmonary edema
Check potassium and ECG urgently when hyperkalemia is suspected
Consider dialysis when there is refractory hyperkalemia, acidosis, volume overload or uremic symptoms

criteria.name: Acute kidney injury after iodinated contrast
criteria.summary: A rise in serum creatinine of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours of contrast administration, or a rise to at least 1.5 times the baseline within 7 days, with no other identified cause of kidney injury.
items: Iodinated contrast given within the preceding 7 days
Creatinine rise of at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours or at least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days
No alternative explanation such as obstruction, sepsis, glomerulonephritis or another nephrotoxin

differential.name: Prerenal azotemia from volume depletion
differential.why_considered: Both cause a rising creatinine after a procedure, and patients who receive contrast are often kept nil by mouth or given diuretics, leaving them hypovolemic.

history: Poor oral intake, vomiting, diarrhea or over-diuresis
No temporal link to contrast, or worsening before the contrast study
exam: Dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor
Postural drop in blood pressure, tachycardia
labs: Creatinine falls quickly after fluid resuscitation
imaging: Normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis on ultrasound

differential.name: Acute tubular necrosis from another cause
differential.why_considered: Ischemic or nephrotoxic tubular injury from hypotension, sepsis or aminoglycosides produces the same muddy brown cast picture and rising creatinine.

history: Prolonged hypotension, sepsis or another nephrotoxin such as gentamicin or amphotericin B
No contrast exposure, or injury already present before contrast
exam: Signs of shock or sepsis: fever, hypotension, warm or cold extremities
labs: Muddy brown granular casts on urinalysis

differential.name: Urinary tract obstruction
differential.why_considered: Obstruction is a common, reversible cause of acute kidney injury in older adults and can follow catheterization or a procedure.
differential.trigger: Oliguria with a palpable bladder, flank pain or a history of prostatic disease, stones or pelvic malignancy

history: Urinary hesitancy, dribbling or a weak stream
Known prostate enlargement, stones or pelvic cancer
labs: Rising creatinine that improves rapidly after catheterization or stenting
imaging: Hydronephrosis or hydroureteronephrosis on renal ultrasound

differential.name: Acute interstitial nephritis
differential.why_considered: Drug-induced interstitial inflammation causes a rising creatinine in hospitalized patients taking multiple medications, including antibiotics and proton pump inhibitors.

history: New medication started days to weeks earlier, such as a beta-lactam, NSAID or proton pump inhibitor
labs: Sterile pyuria with white blood cell casts

differential.name: Acute glomerulonephritis
differential.why_considered: Glomerular disease can present with acute kidney injury and fluid retention, mimicking contrast nephropathy.

history: Recent sore throat or skin infection
Systemic symptoms such as rash, joint pains or hemoptysis
labs: Dysmorphic red blood cells and red blood cell casts on urinalysis
Low complement levels or positive autoantibodies

differential.name: Cholesterol embolization syndrome
differential.why_considered: Follows arterial catheterization, the same setting as contrast nephropathy, and causes acute kidney injury.
differential.trigger: Acute kidney injury after arterial catheterization with livedo reticularis, blue toes or eosinophilia

history: Recent arterial catheterization or vascular surgery
Painful blue toes or skin mottling
exam: Blue or purple toes with intact pulses
labs: Rising creatinine that may not recover

differential.name: Thrombotic microangiopathy
differential.why_considered: Hemolytic anemia with thrombocytopenia and kidney injury can be triggered by medications or occur in hospitalized patients.
differential.trigger: Anemia with thrombocytopenia, schistocytes on smear and rising creatinine

history: Neurologic symptoms such as confusion or headache
labs: Elevated lactate dehydrogenase and indirect bilirubin

differential.name: Atheroembolic renal disease
differential.why_considered: Shares the post-catheterization timing and causes progressive kidney failure.

history: Stepwise decline in kidney function over weeks

severity.mild: Creatinine rises 0.3–0.5 mg/dL above baseline within 48 hours of contrast; urine output preserved; patient feels well or mildly fatigued; no edema or breathlessness.
severity.moderate: Creatinine roughly 1.5–2 times baseline; oliguria may be present; mild dependent edema and weight gain; patient notices reduced urine output and fatigue.
severity.severe: Creatinine more than 2–3 times baseline or above 3 mg/dL; marked oliguria; volume overload with edema, jugular venous distension and crackles; may have hyperkalemia or acidosis.
severity.critical: Anuria or creatinine above 5 mg/dL with refractory hyperkalemia, severe metabolic acidosis, pulmonary edema or uremic encephalopathy; dialysis is required.

red_flags.finding: Urine output less than 0.5 mL/kg/hour for more than 6 hours
red_flags.meaning: Oliguric acute kidney injury; monitor closely and reassess volume status and nephrotoxins

red_flags.finding: Potassium above 6.0 mmol/L or peaked T waves on ECG
red_flags.meaning: Life-threatening hyperkalemia; treat urgently and consider dialysis

red_flags.finding: New crackles, orthopnea or oxygen saturation below 92%
red_flags.meaning: Pulmonary edema from volume overload; may need diuresis or dialysis

red_flags.finding: Creatinine still rising 5–7 days after contrast
red_flags.meaning: Reconsider the diagnosis; look for obstruction, cholesterol emboli or another nephrotoxin

complications.name: Progression to chronic kidney disease
clues: Creatinine does not return to baseline within 1–3 weeks

special_populations.differences: Patients with pre-existing chronic kidney disease have less reserve; a smaller contrast load causes a larger creatinine rise and they are more likely to need dialysis. Prevention with hydration and minimizing contrast volume is most important here.

Diabetic patients often have baseline kidney disease and may have blunted symptoms; the creatinine rise can be mistaken for progression of diabetic nephropathy. Metformin should be held if kidney function worsens because of the risk of lactic acidosis.

May present only with confusion, falls or poor appetite; oliguria is easily missed because urine output is not measured at home. They are also more likely to have heart failure, so fluid resuscitation must be balanced against the risk of pulmonary edema.

Contrast-induced nephropathy is uncommon in children with normal kidneys; when it occurs it follows high-dose contrast for cardiac catheterization or malignancy imaging and presents with reduced urine output.

Iodinated contrast crosses the placenta and fetal thyroid effects are a theoretical concern; use the lowest dose needed and document the indication. Management of acute kidney injury in pregnancy must also consider preeclampsia and HELLP syndrome.

key_questions.question: Have you had a CT scan, angiogram, cardiac catheterization or any other study with contrast dye recently?
key_questions.looking_for: Iodinated contrast exposure within the past 24–72 hours, which is the required trigger for the diagnosis

key_questions.question: When exactly was the contrast given, and when did you first notice less urine or feeling unwell?
key_questions.looking_for: A rise in creatinine or fall in urine output beginning 24–72 hours after contrast, peaking around 3–5 days

key_questions.question: How much are you urinating now compared with before the procedure?
key_questions.looking_for: Oliguria, often first noticed by nursing staff as falling urine output

key_questions.question: Do you know your baseline kidney function, or have you been told your kidneys were weak before?
key_questions.looking_for: Pre-existing chronic kidney disease, which is the strongest risk factor and is needed to interpret the creatinine change

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, heart failure or high blood pressure?
key_questions.looking_for: Diabetes and heart failure, which increase risk and shape fluid management

key_questions.question: Have you been eating and drinking normally, or have you had vomiting, diarrhea or been kept nil by mouth?
key_questions.looking_for: Volume depletion, which worsens injury and is a key alternative or contributing cause

key_questions.question: Which medications do you take, including over-the-counter pain relievers and any new antibiotics?
key_questions.looking_for: Nephrotoxins such as NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, aminoglycosides, vancomycin, amphotericin B, calcineurin inhibitors and cisplatin

key_questions.question: Do you take metformin for diabetes?
key_questions.looking_for: Metformin use, which should be held if kidney function worsens because of the risk of lactic acidosis

key_questions.question: Have you had any fever, chills, burning with urination, flank pain or blood in the urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; these suggest infection, obstruction or glomerulonephritis rather than contrast nephropathy

key_questions.question: Have you noticed swelling in your legs, weight gain, or shortness of breath when lying flat?
key_questions.looking_for: Volume overload from oliguric kidney injury

key_questions.question: Have you had any rash, joint pains, recent sore throat or skin infection?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; these suggest acute interstitial nephritis or glomerulonephritis

key_questions.question: Have you had trouble starting your stream, dribbling, a weak stream or a known enlarged prostate or kidney stones?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present symptoms suggest urinary obstruction, a must-not-miss alternative

key_questions.question: Any confusion, excessive sleepiness or trouble staying alert?
key_questions.looking_for: Uremic encephalopathy, which may require urgent dialysis

key_questions.question: Any muscle weakness, palpitations or a feeling that your heart is skipping?

reasoning_points: Iodinated contrast was given within the preceding 7 days, usually 24–72 hours before the creatinine rise
Serum creatinine rose by at least 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours or to at least 1.5 times baseline within 7 days
Urine output fell, often noticed first by nursing staff as oliguria
Risk factors are present: pre-existing chronic kidney disease, diabetes, older age, heart failure, volume depletion, high contrast volume or concurrent nephrotoxins

Alternative causes are excluded: prerenal azotemia, obstruction, acute tubular necrosis from another cause, acute interstitial nephritis, glomerulonephritis, cholesterol emboli and thrombotic microangiopathy
Urinalysis shows muddy brown granular casts with isosthenuria and only mild proteinuria, without dysmorphic red cells or red cell casts
Renal ultrasound shows normal-sized kidneys without hydronephrosis
The temporal link to contrast and the absence of another explanation are what make the diagnosis

easy: Older patient with chronic kidney disease and diabetes who receives contrast for a CT or cardiac catheterization
Creatinine rises 0.3–0.5 mg/dL about 48 hours after the study
Urine output falls and the patient feels fatigued
No fever, rash, flank pain or dysuria
medium: Patient with volume depletion from poor intake or diuretics, so prerenal azotemia and contrast nephropathy must be separated
Mild pyuria or a few red cells after catheterization that raise concern for infection or glomerular disease
Creatinine rise is attributed to progression of diabetic nephropathy rather than contrast
Patient on multiple nephrotoxins, so the relative contribution of each is unclear
Older adult who presents only with confusion or poor appetite and no measured urine output
hard: Creatinine continues to rise beyond 5–7 days, suggesting cholesterol embolization or another diagnosis
Anemia with thrombocytopenia and schistocytes pointing to thrombotic microangiopathy
Fever, rash and eosinophilia suggesting acute interstitial nephritis
Dysmorphic red cells, red cell casts or heavy proteinuria suggesting glomerulonephritis
Patient with heart failure in whom fluid resuscitation for presumed prerenal disease causes pulmonary edema
Severe hyperkalemia or uremic symptoms requiring urgent dialysis before the diagnosis is fully sorted out
